newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX replies to SIB, seeks changed at LME.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX replies to SIB, seeks changed at LME.

text.p: The New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) has proposed to U.K regulatory watchdog Securities and Investments Board a list of post-Sumitomo London Metals Exchange (LME) reforms because the London exchange "failed to provide meaningful systems to alert, and possibly avoid, the calamitous losses that happened there".
NYMEX president Patrick Thompson dismissed the "party line" that Sumitomo's disgraced trader, Yasuo Hamanaka, lost $2.6 billion through unauthorized trading.
"In our view, indications point more to an actual or attempted market manipulation that failed after years in the making," Thompson said.
The SIB is looking into U.K. trader involvement into the $2.6 billion Sumitomo losses, and whether the workings of the LME need reforming. The SIB is due to report in December.
The scandal sent copper prices crashing, which are only now recovering.

NYMEX suggested seven areas where LME rules should be changed: surveillance, daily pay and collect of variation margins, segregation of customer funds, price transparency, warehouses, conflicts of interest, and information sharing.
Regarding surveillance, large trader reporting and position accountability tools on LME were weaker than on NYMEX, Thompson said.

"The LME seeks to avoid blame for the Sumitomo debacle by claiming that they were unable to obtain this information," Thompson said. "Effective regulation requires both the access to information and the willingness to obtain and use the information."
LME positions should, as is the case already for copper futures traded on NYMEX's Commodity Exchange Inc (COMEX) division, be marked to market in cash to keep them current.
Thompson added that so-called historic price carries on LME allowed customers to roll forward expiring positions and effectively mask the impact of any losses.
NYMEX also told the SIB it knew of no justification for "commingling" of customer funds. "Segregation of funds protects customers, counterparties, and the marketplace," Thompson said.
NYMEX also voiced concern about what it sees as the lack of price transparency on LME, made more acute by addition of LME copper warehouses in the U.S.
"While LME already had a role in pricing world copper, it now, more directly than ever, plays a role in the pricing of U.S. copper," Thompson said.
Regarding warehouses, NYMEX said the physical side of the marketplace must be reviewed to allow for the assessment of the potential for manipulation.
The LME "offers a regulatory approach which seems to protect the interests of powerful players," Thompson told the SIB.
A conflict of interest rose in the LME when governing members were able to set rules ad hoc to limit backwardations, acting on information only available to them.
NYMEX also welcomed steps being taken to ensure greater information sharing between the SIB and its U.S. counterpart, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.
Thompson said that while the SIB did a good job in identifying differences between regulatory regimes, most other exchanges in London were already operating along U.S. regulatory lines.
"The systemic risk created by LME failure to adopt such rules applies equally to those exchanges as to us," Thompson said.
